name: Framemaxxing

lead: Framemaxxing is looksmaxxing shorthand for improving the "frame": shoulder width, clavicle length, ribcage and upper-body mass. The aim is a wider, more V-shaped silhouette, which practitioners say makes a person read as larger and more imposing in person and in photos.

Community guides split the topic into fixed factors (bone structure, height) and modifiable ones (deltoid, trapezius and lat size, posture, body fat, clothing). Some threads also claim that ribcage or scapular expansion techniques can widen the frame; no published study has tested those claims.

paras: Guides describe resistance training that emphasises the shoulders and upper back (overhead presses, lateral raises and similar lifts), keeping body fat low enough for the shoulder-to-waist ratio to show, posture work, and clothing or footwear choices that add visual width or height. Results from muscle training build over months to years.

Muscle training carries ordinary exercise-injury risks. Some framemaxxing threads also list anabolic steroids and human growth hormone as 'hard' routes; those threads themselves note liver, cardiovascular, hormonal and joint risks. Claims that bone width can be expanded in adults are not supported by published studies.

chain: Muscle adds width at shoulder level
angle.text: Training the deltoids, back and traps adds visible width at shoulder level, which increases the shoulder-to-waist contrast that experiments on body shape have found raters respond to. Posture and clothing change how much of that width shows. Bone-width changes are claimed by some guides but are not documented in published research.

lead: Framemaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for maximising the "frame", meaning the visual width and structure of the shoulders, clavicles, ribcage and upper torso. People pursue it to look broader through the upper body and more V-shaped, because a wide shoulder line set against a narrower waist is what practitioners say makes a person read as taller, stronger and more athletic.[1] The word belongs to the same vocabulary as other "-maxxing" practices, which the Wikipedia article on looksmaxxing traces to online forums of the 2010s and to TikTok from the early 2020s.[2]

The route most guides describe is muscular. Training the deltoids, trapezius and latissimus dorsi adds width at shoulder level, and keeping body fat at a level where the waist stays narrow lets that width show.[1][3][4][5] Posture and clothing are added as ways to display the frame. Guides also separate this from the skeleton: height, clavicle length and ribcage dimensions are treated as set largely by genetics and puberty, so the topic is mostly about what is changeable afterwards.[1]

Research on appearance has examined related ideas under other names. Experiments with silhouettes and computer-generated figures have found that men with larger shoulder-to-hip ratios, or lower waist-to-chest ratios, are rated more attractive and more physically capable by raters in the samples studied.[6][7][7] No published study has tested framemaxxing as a defined programme. A second strand of the topic, claims that the ribcage and shoulder blades can be widened in adults by stretching or breathing methods, is discussed on forums but has not been examined in published research.[8]

Height, clavicle length and bone structure (set after skeletal maturity) [1][11]

paras: Frame in looksmaxxing usage refers to the skeleton-plus-muscle outline of the upper body: how wide the shoulders and clavicles are, how deep and wide the ribcage is, and how that compares with the waist and hips. One widely read forum guide calls frame a core component of attractiveness alongside face, height and social skills, and says it is overlooked.[1]

The same guide separates what is set before adulthood (height, clavicle and bone structure) from what stays modifiable, and says a larger underlying frame makes a given amount of muscle look more aesthetic than bulky.[1] Because of that split, most discussion of framemaxxing is discussion of muscle, body fat, posture and presentation. The community uses the word "framecel" for someone who regards their skeletal frame as a limiting factor, and long-running megaguides and annual threads collect advice for them.[9][10]

Anatomy references describe the fixed and changeable parts of the frame. The clavicle is the bony strut that sets much of shoulder breadth; it is usually longer and larger in males, and ossification at its ends finishes late, around 21 to 25 years of age.[11] That is why guides treat bone width as largely settled once growth ends.

The muscular layer sits on top of it. The deltoid has anterior, lateral and posterior heads that converge on the humerus and is the main mover for raising the arm out to the side, so it contributes directly to outline width at shoulder level.[4] The latissimus dorsi is a large fan-shaped back muscle that runs from the lower spine, lower ribs and pelvis to the humerus, and is trained by pull-downs, pull-ups, rows and similar movements; bodybuilders refer to it as the muscle behind back width.[5] Guides therefore pair shoulder work with back work when describing a V-shaped torso.

The megathread's 'softways' list centres on shoulder and upper-back lifting, naming overhead pressing and lateral raises as ways to build deltoid width.[3] Longer guides add diet and body-fat management so that the shoulder-to-waist ratio is visible.[1] Resistance-training references describe muscle growth as responding to training volume, progressive increases in load, and regular repetition of each muscle group over weeks and months, which is why guides frame results as a long-term process.[12]

Guides also treat posture, shoulder position and clothing fit as ways to display the frame. Motion-capture research on men's walking found that lateral torso sway and shoulder abduction were associated with raters' perception of physical dominance.[7]

One thread attributes the broad look of 1950s bodybuilder Steve Reeves to a stretching exercise for the connective tissue around the scapulae combined with ribcage expansion, and proposes a 'Reeves deadlift' routine. The author notes that no proper before-and-after measurements exist.[8] A separate research-style thread collects discussion of clavicles, ribcage and shoulders.[13] Wikipedia's biography of Reeves describes his physique as known for symmetry and records his training as full-body sessions three days a week, without mentioning such a technique.[14]

The megathread's 'hardways' section mentions anabolic steroids and human growth hormone as ways to add muscle, and lists the associated risks in the same post: liver damage, cardiovascular problems and hormonal imbalance for steroids; joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and cancer risk for growth hormone.[3] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists the same substances under 'hardmaxxing'.[2] This wiki gives no dosing or sourcing information.

Proportion has long been a stated goal in physique sport. Bodybuilding competitions are judged on size, conditioning and symmetry, and the Classic Physique division, introduced at Mr. Olympia in 2016, rewards proportion, a small waist and a tapered torso over sheer mass.[15] Steve Reeves (1926 to 2000), who won Mr. America in 1947, Mr. World in 1948 and Mr. Universe in 1950, is the figure forum guides cite most for a wide-shouldered, narrow-waisted look; he later became a film actor and advocated drug-free training.[14][15] Forum guides cite his physique as an example of the frame they describe.[8]

sections.h: Research on shoulders, waist and attractiveness
paras: Wikipedia's summary of the literature says women on average are described as preferring men with a narrow waist, wide chest and broad shoulders, and that waist-to-chest ratio has been reported as the largest determinant of male body attractiveness in some work.[6][16] Fan and colleagues' 2005 study of 69 Chinese and 25 Caucasian male subjects found that overall body volume relative to height explained most of the variance in ratings for young Chinese viewers, with other proportions having smaller but significant effects.[7]

More recent experiments use silhouettes and rendered figures. A 2023 EEG study by Pazhoohi and colleagues reported that larger shoulder-to-hip ratios were rated more attractive by both male and female participants. A second 2023 paper from the same group, covering four studies and 659 heterosexual women, found taller men and men with larger ratios were rated as more attractive, masculine and capable in a fight, with the interaction depending on how realistic the figures were.[7] A 2026 PLoS Biology experiment with over 800 participants rating 343 generated male figures reported selection favouring taller men, more V-shaped bodies and larger penises.[7]

These studies measure the ratio and perceived traits; they do not test frame-building routines. A 2026 study of 176 middle-aged men reported that body composition and adiposity mattered more than shoulder-to-hip ratio-based masculinity for biological-ageing markers, which illustrates that the ratio is used in several research contexts.[7]

Opinion in the forums is divided. Guide authors present frame as unavoidable for dating-market success,[1] while other threads carry titles such as 'does framemaxxing even work', 'do not waste time on frame maxxing' and 'are the botb framemaxxing threads cope', showing an active internal debate about how much of it is changeable.[17][18][19]

Outside the forums, looksmaxxing has been covered by outlets including Business Insider, the New York Times, the BBC and The Guardian, according to Wikipedia, mostly focused on the broader movement rather than frame specifically.[2]

Resistance training carries the ordinary injury risks of lifting, such as strains from poor form or overtraining with low exercise variety and high volume, according to general strength-training references.[12] Anabolic steroid and growth-hormone use, discussed in the 'hardways' threads, carries the risks listed in the same threads: liver, cardiovascular, hormonal and joint effects.[3] No published research has examined the safety of the ribcage or scapula stretching routines described in forum guides.

No studies found. Research on resistance training in general documents muscle growth in trained muscles,[12] and perception studies of shoulder-to-hip ratio are summarised above, but no published trial has tested framemaxxing as a programme or the proposed widening of the ribcage or clavicles in adults.

lore.intro: Framemaxxing threads on looksmax.org range from training guides to debates over whether bone width can change, and several are labelled megaguides or annual threads.[1][9][10]
